title: llm-gemini 0.36
content:
Release: llm-gemini 0.36

Gemini 4 Carbon was announced two weeks ago for "a subset of cyber defenders", but today it's available to everyone else.

This is Google's best ever Gemini, priced at $2/million input and $10/million output at launch (that's GPT-6.1 Sol / Claude Sonnet 5.5 prices) but scheduled to double in price to $4/$20 on December 1st (same as Opus 5.5).

Here are three pelicans for the low, medium and high thinking efforts (it defaults to medium). This is the pelican I got for high:

Gemini pelicans have all been great for a while now, so I also tested it out using Google's Antigravity IDE with a prompt I first tried with Claude Fable 5.2 yesterday:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the HTML result (I had to prompt "build that into a standalone HTML file" to get a version with no external dependencies). I then screen-captured that as a video:

Update: Huh, just saw this on YouTube:

Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music.

title: Glue work is still harmful in the age of AI
content:
I am not a believer in glue work1. Processes that can only be sustained by the unrewarded sacrifice of engineers ought to die.

Now that LLMs are writing most of our code, does that free human engineers up to do more glue work? No, it doesn’t. I think glue work is actually less important to companies than it was in the 2010s. Let’s go through four reasons why.

First, AI decreases the amount of coordination needed to ship. The magnifying effect of AI agents means that any single engineer can now take on projects that would previously have needed a small team. A lot of glue work was helping with coordination: booking kickoff and status meetings, passing around internal updates, and so on. A single engineer doesn’t need to do any of that.

Second, engineers in the 2020s require less “careful handling”. In my experience, the most important subcategory of coordination-based glue work was managing difficult people. Many companies have secret gatekeepers: engineers with outsized influence and large egos who will shoot down your project if they feel insufficiently consulted. I’ve written before about how some teams are structurally set up to be gatekeepers, and how some engineers could get by in the 2010s by basically saying no to everything. The end of ZIRP changed all that. Many of the prickliest gatekeepers have been forced out of the industry or coerced into changing their attitude, which reduces the amount of necessary glue work required to ship.

Third, people are hiring fewer juniors. This is probably a bad thing for the industry, but it does also eliminate a big category of glue work. Experienced hires need less hand-holding, so companies don’t need people to quietly volunteer to onboard new hires.

Fourth, write-only reports can be automated with LLMs. A lot of glue work was what I call “proof of work”: writing a report to demonstrate that you’re aware of what your team is doing, or filling in a template to satisfy some legal requirement. This was often work that nobody wanted to do, so it relied on someone volunteering to “be glue”. Now reports like these can be quickly turned out with LLMs. It doesn’t really matter that nobody wants to read LLM text, because the point of these reports was never to be read anyway.

Can LLMs just automate all glue work? Absolutely not. Many engineers are trying to do this out of a kind of manic optimism, but it’s a really bad idea. Write-only reports are one thing, but communicating to other engineers cannot be delegated to an LLM. When you need to check in on the status of a project, or respond to someone else’s ping, or anything like that, you should compose and write the message yourself. Nothing will torch your relationship with other engineers as quickly as making them talk to your Claude Opus instance.

So where does that leave us? More or less where we were in 2024, I think. Avoid at all costs becoming “the glue work person”, let bad processes fail so they can be changed, but be willing to do small amounts of tactical glue work where it can meaningfully contribute to the success of your projects. Most of your time and effort should still be spent on the code: on driving AI agents and aligning them with your company’s values.

  1. Glue work is all the squishy “non-technical” work that goes into building software: making sure teams are talking to each other, writing reports, updating docs, onboarding engineers, and so on. Specifically it’s the parts of that work that are not included in the formal process, and that only really get done if someone volunteers to do it. For more on why I don’t like it, see my 2024 post Glue work considered harmful.

title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
content:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

title: Gary Marcus: ‘Just Say No to Anthropic’s IPO’
content:
Gary Marcus:

When a business needs exponentially increasing amounts of capital to make modest increases in quality in an intensely competitive market and still owes far more money than it has ever made, there is a serious problem.

I continue to believe that there is no moat in AI models. None. But the entire premise of Anthropic’s IPO is that they have an enormous gulf of a moat.

I would not be shocked to see Anthropic go out of business. Nor would I be shocked if the IPO fails. WeWork tried to IPO, 3 times, and didn’t make it.

I would be surprised if Anthropic does not go out of business. Most cults implode, and Anthropic doesn’t even hide that they’re a cult. And I just don’t see how the math works. Scientology is a long-running cult, but Scientology hasn’t committed $900 billion in spending over the next few years.

(Marcus’s post is on his Substack blog, which, annoyingly, requires you to be logged into a Substack account and to “subscribe”, even though it’s ostensibly a free post. What a rotten oppressive turd of a blogging platform Substack is. Just in case your Substack account isn’t working, here’s a PDF archive.)

title: Book Review: The Unfinished Harauld Hughes - Richard Ayoade ★★★⯪☆
content:
A decade ago, I read Ayoade's first book. In my review, I said:

It's hard to know how to assess a book like this. It's far too clever for its own good - a frustrating and humorous look at... what? It's neither autobiography nor comic novel. An anti-novel which trudges the reader through a series of comic vignettes. It reminded me of some of Woody Allen's work. If you get the joke - you'll find it hilarious. Everyone else will just look on in bemusement.

And, yeah, this new book is pretty much the same! It's an absurdist novel about a (semi) fictional TV presenter creating a documentary about a (probably) fictional director. Much like Bob Mortimer's books it revels in the mundane and delights in uniquely shaped language constructs.

As well as being wryly funny, it is mercilessly satirical. If you've ever read the risible scripts of an "influential" 1950s playwright, you'll immediately feel at home.

There's the drip-feeding of a tiny mystery - but it isn't quite enough to sustain the story. There's no urge to discover what really happened; you'll read this like it was a steam train documentary on in the background while you do the washing-up. There's sort-of a plot-twist, but it is of no consequence.

Despite it's caustic and cynical view about theatre, there are moments of genuine profundity. I found this especially beautiful:

It can sometimes cost ten times as much to sit near the front as compared to the cheap seats in the balcony. And that’s because it’s worth it. The experience is entirely changed by proximity. The tension alters.

What do we want from a celebrity documentary? Is it scandal? Hidden secrets and bitter jealousies? Do we want a behind-the-scenes glimpse at the making-of a documentary? This gets close to being a "Lost in La Mancha" in book form, for an author who didn't exist. It is an enjoyable read, but I think I'd've preferred to watch this late-night on BBC4 never quite knowing if it was a spoof or not.

title: A quick(ish) Chinchilla check
content:
I recently overtrained a couple of GPT-2 style models, training them both on 40 tokens per parameter rather than the 20 per parameter that is generally regarded as "Chinchilla-optimal".

The normal heuristic is that instead of doing that, you should scale up the number of tokens and the number of parameters equally -- so I would have been better off scaling up the model by 2 and the token count by the same amount. By doing that, I should expect to get a better model in terms of loss on my held-back test set than I did with my 40-tokens-per-parameter models.

My training machine poppy wasn't doing anything, so I decided to give that a go. Would the Chinchilla rule-of-thumb hold up?

As you might expect, it did. But it was a surprisingly close-run thing, and could conceivably have been in the noise. Let's take a look.

The Chinchilla heuristic

If you already know all about the Chinchilla paper -- regular readers in particular must be sick and tired of it by now :-) -- then click here to skip this section.

In "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models", which is always called the Chinchilla paper after the name of the model they trained at the end, the authors tried to work out the optimal number of tokens to train an LLM on based on its number of parameters. In particular, they were pushing back on a trend they were seeing at the time, where people were making models ever-larger, but not increasing the amount of data they were training on.

The authors were all at Google DeepMind, and this was the kind of project that only a large lab could do: they trained "over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens". Their conclusion was "for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled".

They don't actually state an overall optimal number of tokens to train on in the paper, but in table 3 they provide an estimate of the optimal training FLOPs and tokens for models of various sizes, and it's approximately 20 tokens per parameter.

That number has become a heuristic, and people talk about a model as being trained for the Chinchilla-optimal number of tokens. Models that were trained on fewer tokens per parameter are referred to as "undertrained", and models that were trained on more as "overtrained".

It's worth noting that overtraining a model is not, in itself, a bad thing. If you have a model of a particular size and you continue training it past the Chinchilla-optimal number of tokens, it will -- in general -- get better. The point of the heuristic is that doing that is not the best way to spend whatever budget you have in terms of compute time. You'll get better results, as they say, by scaling the number of tokens and the number of parameters equally.

But let's say you're creating a model for specific target hardware -- say, a mobile device. You have a hard restriction on how large the model can be -- the device has only so much RAM to hold it. So it might make sense to overtrain to get a better model. 1

But if you're not so limited in how many parameters you can use, then you should indeed scale the model up, and that's what I wanted to try. How would that work?

Scaling the model

A week or two back, I was investigating whether I could make my GPT-2 style models better at a specific instruction-following task by overtraining them. The details of that experiment aren't important here, but what it meant was that I had three GPT-2-style models, each of exactly the same size, roughly 163M parameters

  1. A Chinchilla-optimal one, which I'll call jax-gpt2-chinchilla here.
  2. One trained on twice the Chinchilla-optimal tokens, jax-gpt2-2x-chinchilla.
  3. One trained on the Chinchilla-optimal tokens, with two epochs (so that it was trained for as long as #2): jax-gpt2-2-epoch-chinchilla

When I tested them against a held-back test set of sequences -- stuff that they'd never seen before -- they got results rather like you might expect:

Test loss
jax-gpt2-2x-chinchilla 3.324953
jax-gpt2-2-epoch-chinchilla 3.326482
jax-gpt2-chinchilla 3.418784

A lower loss is better, and you can see that the longer-trained models were noticeably better than the Chinchilla-optimal one. The difference between them was tiny; they were trained starting with the same initial weights, and the training runs themselves were deterministic, but a difference of 0.05% in loss doesn't seem like it could be meaningful -- an extra batch for one or one fewer for the other could easily swap them around, you'd think.

Now, these models each had 163,009,536 parameters -- they were the small-size model from the GPT-2 paper, modified to not have QKV bias or weight-tying. jax-gpt2-chinchilla had been trained on 3,260,190,720 tokens (rounded up to fit into a round number of full batches), and the other two on 6,520,381,440 tokens each -- double the amount (rounded up too).

What I needed to do for my Chinchilla check was to try training a model that used the same amount of compute, scaling the parameters and the number of training tokens equally. Because training compute increases roughly linearly with both parameters and tokens, that would mean scaling both up by 2, giving us:

163,009,536*2≈230,530,296 parameters

...and thus 4,610,605,920 tokens.

How to scale the model up?

In the GPT-2 paper, they train four models:

Name Parameters 2 Layers d_emb MHA heads 3
small 124M 12 768 12
medium 345M 24 1024 16
large 762M 36 1280 20
xl 1542M 48 1600 25

I wanted to scale my own model up from 163M parameters to about 231M. Which of those numbers would I want to increase, and by how much?

The first thing that stands out is that the number of heads is always 1/64th of the number of embedding dimensions. So that sorted that one out. I just needed to adjust the number of layers, and the number of embedding dimensions, but ensure that the latter was a multiple of 64.

I decided to see if I could fit some kind of curve to the relationship between the number of parameters and the GPT-2 authors' choices. This was made a bit more complicated by one thing: they were using weight-tying, and I was not. That meant that they re-used the embedding matrix at the start of the LLM as an output head at the end -- which is why they had 38M fewer parameters. Embeddings and the output head make up a surprisingly large percentage of the parameters for small models like this -- about 47% without weight-tying, 23% with.

I couldn't work out a solid way to scale things up and wound up doing some rather messy hacking around in a spreadsheet. I came up with two proposed model sizes that were within a couple of percentage points of the right size:

Name Layers d_emb MHA heads Parameters % diff
slightly-larger 15 896 14 235,621,120 +2.21%
slightly-smaller 14 896 14 225,978,368 -1.97%

Interestingly, I found that because d_emb could only change in increments/decrements of 64, it was a pretty coarse control -- my first attempt at making a slightly-smaller model changed it to the next step down, 832, but that led to a model that was 9.25% too small.

That was an interesting first lesson. I'd previously been thinking of the Chinchilla rule as being something like "don't double the tokens, just scale the model and the tokens equally". But that "just" was wrong. Scaling a model is hard -- even with just two dials to fiddle with, like in this case, it was tricky to get something right -- and I can't say for sure that my choices were the right ones.

Anyway, the next step was to double-check that these models would use the right amount of compute to train.

Training FLOPs

As I said earlier, the compute time scales roughly linearly with the number of parameters. Let's dig into that "roughly".

Different kinds of parameters take different amounts of FLOPs to train, and scale differently with things like the embedding dimensions, sequence length, and so on.

Now, for very large models, a lot of that comes out in the wash, but with tiny models like these where the embeddings make up such a large proportion of the parameters, it might matter.

Conveniently, in appendix F of the Chinchilla paper, they provide a set of formulae for estimating the number of training FLOPs for a normal dense LLM like these ones. I coded that up into a script that, given the JSON configuration files I was using for my models and training runs, would work out the number of FLOPs for a single epoch of training. It didn't take account of the fact that my real training runs round the number of tokens up so that we do a round number of full batches, but I felt that so long as the results weren't very close that wouldn't matter.

I got these results (multiplying the two-epoch numbers by two):

Est. training FLOPs
jax-gpt2-chinchilla 3,544,967,596,946,227,200
jax-gpt2-2x-chinchilla 7,089,935,193,892,454,400
jax-gpt2-2-epoch-chinchilla 7,089,935,193,892,454,400
slightly-larger 7,419,664,885,127,577,600
slightly-smaller 6,804,429,215,367,168,000

The numbers were indeed different enough that I wasn't worried about the batch-rounding. And the good news was that slightly-larger and slightly-smaller would indeed use slightly more and slightly less compute to train than the overtrained models -- about 4.6% more and 4% less respectively. A true Chinchilla-equivalent model would lie somewhere between them.

It was time to train some models!

Training

I kicked off the run for the slightly-larger model first. Because it was bigger than the 163M models I'd been training, I couldn't fit such large batches into my VRAM; previously I'd been running with a batch size of 6, and now I could only fit in a batch of 4. Luckily, though, I was using gradient accumulation, so by bumping that up from 16 steps to 24 steps I could keep the same overall batch size and keep the training runs comparable.

Even despite that, the training run ran out of VRAM about 60 hours in -- I'm guessing due to VRAM fragmentation, as I did not have TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR set to cuda_malloc_async -- but I was able to restart from the most recent checkpoint and complete the run. After just less than four days total training time, it completed.

When it was done, I copied the last checkpoint 4 over to my dev box, perry, and ran my standard smoke test against it, asking it to complete "Every effort moves you" with 20 tokens, using greedy sampling. I got something reasonably coherent:

Every effort moves you.
I’m not sure what you’re thinking.
I’m

Next, I converted the safetensors file -- which had been saved by my JAX code -- into a format compatible with my PyTorch code, because that's what I use for evals. I ran another smoke test (this one with temperature 1):

Every effort moves you through the motions for your life, your soul, your body,
and your soul’s happiness

Very spiritual. Next, it was time to work out the loss on my held-back test set:

giles@perry:~/Dev/ddp-base-model-from-scratch (main)$ uv run test_loss.py datasets/ ../jax-gpt2-from-scratch/runs/full-llm-full-train-with-mha-output-bias-larger-chinchilla/model.json ../jax-gpt2-from-scratch/runs/full-llm-full-train-with-mha-output-bias-larger-chinchilla/checkpoints/latest/pytorch-model.safetensors
Fetching 4 files: 100%|███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 4/4 [00:00<00:00, 3485.09it/s]
100%|█████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 3200/3200 [07:11<00:00,  7.42it/s]
Loss against our test dataset: 3.280028

Well, it was certainly better than the 3.324953 that the best of the overtrained models got -- but only by a bit over 1% better. Interesting!

Update: The model is now on Hugging Face as gpjt/jax-with-mha-bias-larger-chinchilla-1.

I decided to train the second model, slightly-smaller. This one crashed mid-way through with an error that I've seen before:

jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: INTERNAL: CUDA error: Failed to end stream capture: CUDA_ERROR_STREAM_CAPTURE_INVALIDATED: operation failed due to a previous error during capture [executable_name='jit_train_step']

I'm going to have to investigate that more in future, but for now, I just restarted from the checkpoint, and again after a bit less than four days, I had a model.

The JAX smoke test was solid:

Every effort moves you forward.
The best way to get started is to start with a free trial.
You can

...and so was the PyTorch one:

Every effort moves you forward in love with our products.
I love the way it’s easy to use.

Both quite commercial this time! It was time for the proper test loss eval:

giles@perry:~/Dev/ddp-base-model-from-scratch (main)$ uv run test_loss.py datasets/ ~/Dev/jax-gpt2-from-scratch/runs/full-llm-full-train-with-mha-output-bias-larger-chinchilla-2/model.json ~/Dev/jax-gpt2-from-scratch/runs/full-llm-full-train-with-mha-output-bias-larger-chinchilla-2/checkpoints/latest/pytorch-model.safetensors
Fetching 4 files: 100%|███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 4/4 [00:00<00:00, 3151.24it/s]
100%|█████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| 3200/3200 [06:45<00:00,  7.90it/s]
Loss against our test dataset: 3.292937

So, slightly worse than the 3.280028 from the larger model, better than the 3.324953 from the best overtrained one.

Update: The model is now on Hugging Face as gpjt/jax-with-mha-bias-larger-chinchilla-2.

Time to put this all together.

Results

Here's an updated version of the table from the start of this post; I've added in the two new models, and the improvement they each had over jax-gpt2-2x-chinchilla in both absolute terms and as a percentage rounded to 3sf.

Test loss Improvement Improvement %
slightly-larger 3.280028 0.044925 1.35%
slightly-smaller 3.292937 0.032016 0.962%
jax-gpt2-2x-chinchilla 3.324953 - -
jax-gpt2-2-epoch-chinchilla 3.326482 - -
jax-gpt2-chinchilla 3.418784 - -

Now, unlike the overtrained models, prior to training these two new ones started with different initial weights to the jax-gpt2-chinchilla one -- after all, they had to, because they had more of them!

A while back, I did a bit of analysis of how random variation in weight initialisation can change the resulting test loss. It wasn't anything in-depth, but I trained three models with different explicit seeds set prior to the model initialisation, but with the same seed set before the training run started 5.

Those three models wound up with test losses of 3.681356, 3.673943, and 3.664345. Doing statistics with three data points is a bit flaky, but the cost of training models is so high that I'll leave the Proper Science to the likes of Google DeepMind and wing it :-)

  • Mean: ~3.673215
  • Sample variance: ~0.000073
  • Standard deviation (SD): ~0.008529

Now, piling statistical flakiness on statistical flakiness, we'll compare these. You'd normally expect about two thirds of results to be within one SD of the mean, 95.4% to be within two SDs, and 99.7% to be within three.

Three SDs on that (yes, different, I know) distribution is 0.025587. That's smaller than both of the improvements that our Chinchilla-optimal runs had over the overtrained ones.

So what does that tell us? Well, perhaps not much given the statistical flakiness. But I think it is useful directionally. It suggests that we might be able to take these results seriously as an improvement, and that Chinchilla held: scaling up the model and the number of tokens evenly did give us a better model than just scaling up the number of tokens. In particular, the fact that the loss for slightly-smaller was lower -- even though it had 4% less compute spent on it than the overtrained models -- was encouraging.

But it's certainly far from a slam-dunk. A larger test, training lots of overtrained models and lots of Chinchilla-optimal ones, all with different random seeds, would give actual real serious data.

Not worth it for me, and perhaps not for anyone.

Conclusion

I wanted to do a quick sanity check of the Chinchilla heuristic of 20 tokens per parameter. I came up with results that were certainly in line with it -- perfectly so in terms of the ordering of the models I trained. But the effect was small enough that I could imagine that it was in the noise, especially given the small numbers of models I'm able to train. I'll chalk it up as a tentative success.

In addition, I learned one useful thing: when talking about scaling up a model to more parameters, you actually have to think quite hard about where you want to put those parameters. I wound up doing a rough curve-fit to the models in the GPT-2 paper, but I have no idea if that was optimal. At some point I should try to dig up some research into optimising embedding dimensions, numbers of layers, and so on. But not now, as I've a bunch of other stuff I want to investigate first.

Anyway, I hope you found this experiment interesting, and as ever, comments and questions welcome below. Thanks for reading!

  1. I'm less familiar with arguments for under-training -- that is, for fewer than 20 tokens per parameter. I've heard that these days, modern LLMs get a lot more reinforcement learning than they do pre-training, and perhaps that might mean that some very big ones are undertrained prior to RL? I'm uncertain. It's unlikely to be raw lack of data; even for those of us outside the big labs, FineWeb has 18.5T tokens. On its own, that would be enough to train a 0.925T-parameter model, and given that you can apparently do four epochs over the same data before you start getting diminishing returns, that takes us up to 3.7T. That's frontier-lab size, and I'm sure they have better datasets than FineWeb. ↩

  2. Parameter counts are from the paper, apart from the "small" model, which is known to be wrong -- I used my own calculation, and the result is in line with what I've seen elsewhere. ↩

  3. The paper doesn't mention the number of heads; these numbers are from "Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)", and match up with the ones on this Hugging Face page. ↩

  4. Regular readers might have noticed that I'm ignoring what I've been calling the "best" checkpoint. I've come to the conclusion that because for my training script, "best" means best in terms of training loss, and the training loss changes based on what training data the model has seen recently, it's actually not a very useful metric and just confuses things. At some point I'll probably re-introduce pre-checkpoint evals and use that for "best", which would be the right way to do it. ↩

  5. At the time I was using dropout, so training runs were not deterministic without a known seed. ↩
description: I recently overtrained a couple of GPT-2 style models, training them both on 40 tokens per parameter rather than the 20 per parameter that is generally regarded as "Chinchilla-optimal". The normal heuristic is that instead of doing that, you should scale up the number of tokens and the number of parameters equally -- so I would have been better off scaling up the model by 2 and the token count by the same amount. By doing that, I should expect to get a better model in terms of loss on my held-ba

title: Monads in Lean
content:
This post demonstrates how to use monads in the Lean programming language (Lean 4, to be specific). If you're not familiar with Lean, this part of the language is very similar to other functional programming languages, like Haskell or OCaml.

Motivating example - evaluating expressions

Suppose we want to write a simple numerical expression evaluator that supports numbers with addition and division:

inductive Expr where
  | num : Int → Expr
  | add : Expr → Expr → Expr
  | div : Expr → Expr → Expr

What happens when we encounter a division by zero? We'll want our evaluator to report this as a failure, which will be represented explicitly using the the Option type:

def safeDiv (x y : Int) : Option Int :=
  if y == 0 then none else some (x / y)

With this in hand, the eval function can be written as follows:

def eval : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => some n
  | .add a b =>
    match eval a with
    | none => none
    | some x =>
      match eval b with
      | none => none
      | some y => some (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    match eval a with
    | none => none
    | some x =>
      match eval b with
      | none => none
      | some y => safeDiv x y

safeDiv returns an Option; to propagate that possible failure to its caller, eval also returns an Option, and - moreover - has to perform lots of tedious checking for the possibility of a none value. Is there a better way?

Note a common code pattern repeated here:

  1. Examine the value of an Option
  2. If it's none, return none without proceeding
  3. Otherwise if it's some result, continue the computation with result

We can extract it into a helper function:

def withSome (result : Option α) (onSuccess : α → Option β) : Option β :=
  match result with
  | none => none
  | some x => onSuccess x

And rewrite our eval using this helper:

def evalWithSome : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => some n
  | .add a b =>
      withSome (evalWithSome a) (fun x =>
        withSome (evalWithSome b) (fun y =>
          some (x + y)))
  | .div a b =>
      withSome (evalWithSome a) (fun x =>
        withSome (evalWithSome b) (fun y =>
          safeDiv x y))

This is already much better; we can make it even cleaner using operator overloading:

infixl:55 " >>? " => withSome

def evalOp : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => some n
  | .add a b =>
    evalOp a >>? fun x =>
    evalOp b >>? fun y =>
    some (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    evalOp a >>? fun x =>
    evalOp b >>? fun y =>
    safeDiv x y

Congratulations - we've pretty much invented monads!

Option as a Monad in expression evaluation

In simplified form, the Monad type class in Lean is defined as:

class Monad (m : Type → Type) where
  pure : α → m α
  bind : m α → (α → m β) → m β

In our code, pure is equivalent to some, and bind is equivalent to withSome; in fact, the Monad instance for Option is something like:

instance : Monad Option where
  pure x := some x
  bind opt next :=
    match opt with
    | none => none
    | some x => next x

An operator akin to >>? for monads is already defined in Lean; it's called >>=, and picks up the bind method of the Monad type class. So we can rewrite our evaluator using the standard Monad instance, without defining withSome or the >>? operator [1]:

def evalBind : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b =>
    evalBind a >>= fun x =>
    evalBind b >>= fun y =>
    some (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    evalBind a >>= fun x =>
    evalBind b >>= fun y =>
    safeDiv x y

We can go even further with the do notation, which is syntactic sugar around >>= that lets us rewrite the evaluator as:

def evalDo : Expr → Option Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalDo a
    let y ← evalDo b
    some (x + y)
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalDo a
    let y ← evalDo b
    safeDiv x y

This notation should be familiar if you've seen Lean code dealing with I/O; we'll revisit I/O later in the post.

Monads for modeling side effects

Functional programming languages place a lot of emphasis on pure functions that are free of side effects. There's no question that such functions are easier to reason about, debug, and even optimize (by memoization). That said, the real world is messy and sometimes side effects are inescapable; monads help encapsulate side effects in functional programs.

The core idea is: side effects are encapsulated inside a Monad, which wraps the value returned from a computation. The bind method (or the equivalent >>= operator) lets us take a wrapped value and push it into the next computation in the sequence. This may look familiar from continuation-passing style (CPS). Continuations themselves can also be modeled with a monad [2].

The definition of bind is:

bind : m α → (α → m β) → m β

Here's a mental model to think about it:

  1. Take a value wrapped with potential side effects
  2. Take a computation that takes this value and may produce additional side effects
  3. Combine the results into a final wrapped value

Chaining multiple binds together is essentially a sequence of computations while keeping track of the side effects. A monad decouples what computations do from how they are sequenced. The programmer describes the sequence of computations and their dependencies, while the monad's bind implementation handles the bookkeeping necessary to combine their side effects.

Our evaluator case study shows one example of side effects: early return from a computation with a none value.

Let's see another idiomatic way of doing that, with the Except type that contains either a successful result or an error value (very similar to the Result type in Rust).

We'll begin by writing an exception-returning version of safeDiv:

def safeDivExc (x y : Int) : Except String Int :=
  if y == 0 then .error "division by zero" else .ok (x / y)

Instead of writing a whole new eval variant for Except, we'll create a generic one that works with any Monad [3]:

def evalM {m : Type → Type} [Monad m]
    (div : Int → Int → m Int) : Expr → m Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b =>
    do
      let x ← evalM div a
      let y ← evalM div b
      pure (x + y)
  | .div a b =>
    do
      let x ← evalM div a
      let y ← evalM div b
      div x y

Now evalM can be used with safeDivExc to implement an evaluator where division returns Except; used with safeDiv, it would be equivalent to the Option-specific evalDo we've written before.

#eval evalM safeDiv (.add (.num 4) (.div (.num 6) (.num 0)))
#eval evalM safeDivExc (.add (.num 4) (.div (.num 6) (.num 0)))

Logging computations - an example of the writer monad

Let's look at a more advanced example: an evaluator that also logs the computation it executes in a linear log of strings. The challenge here is that we still have to combine that with Option to support the divide-by-zero case, so we'll start by creating a new structure to carry the state of the computation:

structure LoggedOption (α : Type) where
  value : Option α
  log : List String

This will be the result of one eval call; it produces an optional value, along with a list of strings (the log). Here's the Monad implementation for this type:

instance : Monad LoggedOption where
  pure x := ⟨some x, []⟩
  bind v next :=
    match v.value with
    | none => ⟨none, v.log⟩
    | some x =>
      let nextResult := next x
      ⟨nextResult.value, v.log ++ nextResult.log⟩

The main idea is combining the stored log with the log of the next computation by appending them (thus accumulating a linear log). Here's our evaluator:

def evalLogged : Expr → LoggedOption Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalLogged a
    let y ← evalLogged b
    ⟨some (x + y), [s!"adding {x} and {y}"]⟩
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalLogged a
    let y ← evalLogged b
    match y with
    | 0 => ⟨none, [s!"dividing {x} by zero"]⟩
    | _ => ⟨some (x / y), [s!"dividing {x} by {y}"]⟩

Note how the code of evalLogged doesn't have to deal with the mechanics of logging too much (other than adding new log entries). All of that is hidden within the monad instance. LoggedOption is an example of the writer monad, which is a write-only version of the state monad.

State monad

One of the most important use cases of monads in functional programming languages is modeling mutable state through a computation.

A stateful computation is modeled as a function that takes an initial state and returns a tuple containing the result value and a new, updated state. In Lean notation:

def State (σ : Type) (α : Type) : Type :=
  σ → (α × σ)

To demonstrate this in action, let's enhance our evaluator to support variable assignments and lookups. Our state is going to be an association list of name, value pairs:

abbrev Vars := List (String × Int)

And we'll augment our expression enum with additional operations:

inductive ExprV where
  | num : Int → ExprV
  | add : ExprV → ExprV → ExprV
  | div : ExprV → ExprV → ExprV
  | store : String → ExprV → ExprV
  | load : String → ExprV

This is going to be our state monad:

structure EvalM (α : Type) where
  run : Vars → Option (α × Vars)

Note the correspondence of the run function to the State signature above:

  • It takes the current state, which for our use cases is an association list carrying values for all defined variables.
  • It returns an optional result which is a pair of some value (in our case, the result of the computation) and an updated state.

This is its Monad class implementation:

instance : Monad EvalM where
  pure x := ⟨fun vars => some (x, vars)⟩
  bind action next := ⟨fun vars =>
    match action.run vars with
    | none => none
    | some (x, vars') => (next x).run vars'⟩

And finally, the evaluator:

def evalState : ExprV → EvalM Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalState a
    let y ← evalState b
    pure (x + y)
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalState a
    let y ← evalState b
    ⟨fun vars => (safeDiv x y).map (fun value => (value, vars))⟩
  | .load name =>
    ⟨fun vars => do
      let value ← vars.lookup name
      pure (value, vars)⟩
  | .store name rhs => do
    let value ← evalState rhs
    ⟨fun vars =>
      let vars' := (name, value) :: vars.filter (fun p => p.1 != name)
      some (value, vars')⟩

Operations that don't deal with variables directly (like .num and .add) just do their work as before. .div only has to deal with the actual monad type to ensure that none is propagated in case of division by zero. Note also that this evaluator supports stores as expressions, since they separately return a value and the updated state; therefore, computations like this one will work:

-- (x := 12) + (x / 3): the right operand sees the left operand's assignment.
#eval (evalState
  (.add (.store "x" (.num 12))
        (.div (.load "x") (.num 3)))).run []

Producing the result some (16, [("x", 12)]).

In a language with mutable state, modeling side effects is easy - just assign some state (like a struct field or class member). In a functional language like Lean, however, we have to carry this state across the computations explicitly; monads help us do this with elegance - by hiding most of the mechanics of actually carrying the state around, the majority of the code remains free of bookkeeping.

IO monad

Perhaps the most well known example of a monad in functional programming languages like Lean and Haskell is IO. To anyone who's written a "real" program that interacts with the outer world, IO is very familiar. Here's a customized "Hello" program that's typically taught in the first 15 minutes of learning a new programming language:

def greet : IO Unit := do
  let stdin ← IO.getStdin
  IO.println "What is your name?"
  let name ← stdin.getLine
  IO.println s!"Hello, {name}"

Note the do notation here, suggesting monads. As mentioned before, do is syntactic sugar for the monad's bind method, or the >>= operator; we can rewrite this code more explicitly as:

def greetBind : IO Unit :=
  IO.getStdin >>= fun stdin =>
  IO.println "What is your name?" >>= fun _ =>
  stdin.getLine >>= fun name =>
  IO.println s!"Hello, {name}"

In essence, IO is a state monad, where the state carried around represents the "outside world". IO operations like println act on that world, and its state is carried over using bind, like other state monads.

Here's a version of our expression evaluator that logs directly to standard out, instead of collecting the log as a list of strings:

def evalIO : Expr → OptionT IO Int
  | .num n => pure n
  | .add a b => do
    let x ← evalIO a
    let y ← evalIO b
    IO.println s!"adding {x} and {y}"
    pure (x + y)
  | .div a b => do
    let x ← evalIO a
    let y ← evalIO b
    IO.println s!"dividing {x} by {y}"
    OptionT.mk (pure (safeDiv x y))

The only unusual construct here is OptionT, which is a monad transformer that helps us compose Option (for propagating failure from safe division) with the IO Monad [4].

The IO monad also supports throw for Python-like exception behavior, but in this example we use Option explicitly; exceptions are a matter of programming preference, and using them inside library functions like eval doesn't feel right to me.

Monad laws in Lean

Just like in Haskell, monads in Lean should obey certain laws. Those are:

Left identity: wrapping a value in pure and immediately passing it to f with bind should be equivalent to just calling f on the value:

pure v >>= f       =    f v

Right identity: extracting a value from a computation and immediately wrapping it with pure again should not change the computation:

m >>= pure         =    m

Associativity: the grouping of operations doesn't matter, as long as their order remains the same:

(m >>= f) >>= g    =    m >>= (fun v => f v >>= g)

Let's see how Option obeys these laws.

For left identity, pure v is some v and the bind implementation matches some x to next x, which is equivalent to f v.

For right identity, m >>= pure just rewraps a some value in pure, leaving none alone - this is equivalent to keeping things as they are.

For associativity, if m is none then both sides are none. If m is some v, the left side is f v >>= g, and the right side reduces to the same, so again they are equivalent.

While Lean doesn't enforce that a Monad instance obeys these laws, it has a separate type class called LawfulMonad which does require Lean proofs; this is useful for Lean's main use case - proving theorems about programs, expressed through its powerful type system. But this is a topic for another day.

[1]We've replaced some n by pure n in the .num case; technically this isn't necessary, but it will be useful later in the post when we examine other types implementing Monad.
[2]This is explored in Philip Wadler's classical paper "The essence of functional programming".
[3]Except also happens to implement Monad.
[4]We could also have used OptionT in earlier examples, e.g. instead of explicitly defining LoggedOption - try changing that code to use OptionT as an exercise.

title: Finally, Payment by Bank Transfer Comes to Have I Been Pwned
content:
This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

  1. Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢
  2. Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.
